cards.heading: 128 bits in hex
cards.body: An IPv6 address is 128 bits written as eight groups (hextets) of four hex digits. The usual split is a 64-bit prefix (network) and a 64-bit interface ID. An ISP typically hands a site a /48, which leaves 16 bits for subnets: 65,536 /64 subnets.

cards.heading: Shortening addresses
cards.body: Two rules: drop leading zeros in each group, and replace one run of consecutive all-zero groups with ::. Use :: only once (otherwise the address is ambiguous), on the longest run; if two runs tie, the first. A single zero group stays as 0. This is the RFC 5952 canonical form: leading zeros must go, letters are lower case, and :: replaces the longest run (the first run on a tie).

cards.heading: Global unicast and unique local
cards.body: Global unicast addresses (2000::/3, so they start with 2 or 3) are public and routable, like public IPv4. Unique local addresses (FC00::/7, in practice FDxx) are private, like RFC 1918. Unique local addresses with the L bit set fall in FD00::/8, followed by a random 40-bit global ID. LAN subnets normally use a /64, which leaves the 64-bit interface ID that SLAAC and EUI-64 need; /48 and /56 are typical site allocations, and /128 is a single address.

cards.heading: Link-local
cards.body: Every IPv6 interface creates a link-local address in FE80::/10 by itself. It's only valid on that link and never routed. Routers use link-local addresses as next hops and to send Router Advertisements.

cards.heading: Multicast and anycast
cards.body: IPv6 has no broadcast. Multicast addresses start with FF: FF02::1 all nodes, FF02::2 all routers, FF02::5/6 OSPF, FF02::1:FFxx:xxxx solicited-node (used by Neighbor Discovery instead of ARP). Anycast is one unicast address configured on several devices; packets go to the nearest one.

cards.heading: Modified EUI-64
cards.body: A host or router can build its 64-bit interface ID from its MAC address: split the MAC in half, insert FFFE, and flip the 7th bit (the U/L bit) of the first byte.

cards.heading: Configuring a router
cards.body: Routing IPv6 must be turned on globally. Interfaces can get a manual address, an EUI-64 address or just a link-local address. Hosts can learn their prefix from Router Advertisements (SLAAC) or use DHCPv6. With SLAAC the host takes the /64 prefix from the Router Advertisement and adds its own interface ID (EUI-64 or random). Neighbor Discovery (NDP) replaces ARP for finding MAC addresses.
cards.example:
ipv6 unicast-routing
interface g0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
interface g0/1
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64

cards.heading: Special addresses
cards.body: ::1 is loopback and :: (all zeros) is unspecified, used as a source before an address is assigned.
